Advertising Rates made known on application.

Standing Advertisements payable quarterly.

Address all communications to THE BAD LANDS COW BOY, MEDORA, DAKOTA.

articles.headline: MEDORA.
articles.text:
We have before spoken of Medora's future, but it is a subject of which we cannot say too much. We never have and never will indulge in the boom-fizz-Pat-Donan style of literary architecture, but now and at all times will deal in facts and from them gain our conclusions.

It is a well-known fact that a cattle town is livelier and wealthier than an agricultural town. Medora is not and never by any possibility can be an agricultural town. That she will be a great cattle town is beyond all question. We state boldly and without fear of successful challenge that the Bad Lands are the best cattle country in the United States. This is readily proved by the greater per cent. of increase and less per cent. of loss that we enjoy, in comparison to any other cattle region. The cattle country tributary to Medora is already more than a hundred by fifty miles and the extent that will be tributary is almost unlimited. This is for the reason that Medora is the only place that has east, west, north and south outlets. In addition to this, we have the one thing that would force a town to grow here even if we had not the location. That is, a market. In the course of time, the N. P. R. C. Co. will buy for killing or shipping, every animal on the river. From this will arise the inevitable factories that the extensive abattoirs soon to be built, will amply support.

Almost without the cattle the location itself is enough to build a town, or it is an exception to a rule, hitherto invariable. Take any east and west rail-road in the country, follow its course and it will be found that at the crossing of every stream that has a supply of water the year round, there springs up a good town. This is the case whether the stream is navigable or not. Take the N. P., for instance, to this point. St. Paul and Minneapolis are virtually at one crossing of the Mississippi and Brainerd is at the other. Moorhead and Fargo are on the Red river, Jamestown on the James and Bismarck and Mandan on the Missouri. Although these are all larger rivers than the Little Missouri, the rule still holds good in all cases.

We will not stop here however, for the freight route and coming rail-road place the Black Hills and southern Bad Lands tributary to us and makes Medora the capital of a larger and far richer country than any of the cities mentioned. This will also make Medora a great jobbing point and to this, the cattle industries and the freight route we will owe a prosperity as phenomenal as it is sure.
articles.summary: Packard argues Medora will be a great cattle town and jobbing point thanks to the Bad Lands range, the N. P. R. C. Co. market and abattoirs, its river-crossing location, and the Black Hills freight route.

articles.text: The new agent, Mr. Brinker, came yesterday to relieve Mr. Spurrier.
articles.summary: Mr. Brinker arrived as the new railroad agent, relieving Mr. Spurrier.

articles.text: A large number of sheep pelts were brought in yesterday from Beaumont's ranch.
articles.summary: Sheep pelts were brought in from Beaumont's ranch.

articles.text: There is not a better opening on the line of the road for a shoemaker than Medora.
articles.summary: The paper says Medora offers an opening for a shoemaker.

articles.text: Mr. Morrison, who has a fine lot of young cattle on Beaver creek, has been in town for several days.
articles.summary: Mr. Morrison, who has young cattle on Beaver creek, has been in town for several days.

articles.text: Mr. Weatherby, of Mandan, travelling for Charlie VanSlyck, was in town yesterday. He started east this morning.
articles.summary: Mr. Weatherby of Mandan, travelling for Charlie VanSlyck, visited and went east.

articles.text: Dr. McIntosh, of Glendive, was in town Tuesday, attending Mrs. Fitzgerald's baby, which was quite sick the first of the week.
articles.summary: Dr. McIntosh of Glendive came Tuesday to attend Mrs. Fitzgerald's sick baby.

articles.text: The billiard hall is rapidly approaching completion. In fifteen days at the farthest, Pennell & Roberts expect to open it with a grand ball.
articles.summary: Pennell & Roberts expect to open their nearly finished billiard hall with a grand ball within fifteen days.

articles.text: A good deal of work is being done toward the establishment of the stage route and we expect to see it in full running operation in less than a month.
articles.summary: Work toward the stage route is going on; it is expected to run within a month.

articles.text: We are reliably informed that the plan of building the rail-road to the Hills is being energetically pushed and that in all probabitity work will begin this summer.
articles.summary: The paper hears the railroad to the Black Hills is being pushed and work may begin this summer.

articles.text: Wm. Jones returned the first of the week from his hunt after Charlie Jolly's horses. He corralled three of them and heard that the fourth had been seen on the way to the Hills.
articles.summary: Wm. Jones recovered three of Charlie Jolly's lost horses; the fourth was seen heading to the Hills.

articles.text: Freight is coming in on almost every train and the freight house will soon be badly needed. The brick will soon be ready however, and the building will begin immediately.
articles.summary: Freight is arriving on most trains; the brick freight house will be begun as soon as brick is ready.

articles.text: We have sold a number more valuable lots this week and purchasers will begin to come in rapidly, judging from the letters we are receiving from prospective purchasers and business men.
articles.summary: The Cow Boy sold more town lots this week.

articles.text: Smith & Graham's outfit loaded yesterday and will start to-day or to-morrow for the Hills. One of the wagons is an immense affair, the hind wheels being six feet high and the tires are an inch thick.
articles.summary: Smith & Graham's outfit loaded for the Black Hills; one wagon has six-foot hind wheels.

articles.text: Over four thousand pounds of deer and antelope hides came in from Spearfish this morning, for McFarland & Kyes. They came over the new freight route and the freighters report the road in splendid condition.
articles.summary: Over 4,000 pounds of deer and antelope hides arrived from Spearfish for McFarland & Kyes over the new freight route.

articles.text: In addition to the large lot of cattle brought in by Gregor Lang, another lot will arrive soon. As stated in a former issue, Mr. Lang will soon build a substantial dwelling on his home ranch and bring his family here.
articles.summary: Gregor Lang expects another lot of cattle and will build a dwelling on his home ranch and bring his family.

articles.text: J. C. Fisher and Wm. Vandriesche will soon begin the erection of a building for business purposes. It will contain three store rooms and as tenants are waiting already, it will not only be a needed but a profitable improvement.
articles.summary: J. C. Fisher and Wm. Vandriesche will erect a business building with three store rooms.

articles.text: The lumber is now on the way for three dwelling houses, which will be built immediately on its arrival. The reason for the haste is that families are already here awaiting the buildings. The rest of them will probably be built of brick.
articles.summary: Lumber is on the way for three dwelling houses for families already waiting; later houses will likely be brick.

articles.text: The lettering on the COW BOY roof is a subject of profound meditation and anxious inquiry on the part of emigrants passing through. One emigrant was heard to remark that it must be a pretty tough cow-boy that they put on exhibition in this country.
articles.summary: Emigrants passing through puzzle over the lettering on the Cow Boy roof.

articles.text: T. J. Kerr will be here to-morrow or Saturday. His duties as auditor of the N. P. R. C. Co. will keep him on the road until the books of all the cold-storage houses are started, after which he will be found at the Medora headquarters the most of the time. As soon as he gets settled he will bring his family out.
articles.summary: T. J. Kerr, auditor of the N. P. R. C. Co., is due and will later base himself at Medora and bring his family.

articles.text: Additions will be made to the abattoir as soon as work is finished on the billiard hall. Facilities for slaughtering a hundred more head a day will be added to satisfy the large contracts entered into by the Marquis in New York. Full work will not begin much before June 1, as the cattle are not yet in prime condition.
articles.summary: The abattoir will be enlarged by a hundred head a day to meet the Marquis's New York contracts; full work to begin about June 1.

articles.text: We are afraid that after all we are destined not to have Dr. Louthan as a citizen, for a time at least. He fully intended coming from Spearfish with Mr. Jones and had taken his seat in the buckboard for that purpose, when almost the whole town turned out and actually forced him to stay. Better luck next time, Dr.
articles.summary: Dr. Louthan was kept at Spearfish when the town there turned out and stopped him from leaving for Medora.

articles.headline: SPORTING NOTES.
articles.text: [Not transcribed in full: clipped national sporting paragraphs.] Items concern Hanlan and Laycock rowing at Sydney, N. S. W., May 22; Malone at pool in New York; bicycle polo at Washington; roller skating and roller polo; John Hughes and Fitzgerald; cricket clubs in the east; a collar-and-elbow wrestling match at Chicago May 3; the League of American Wheelmen meeting in Washington; Woodside & Morgan's trans-continental bicycle trip ("It is a good thing for them that the Bad Lands are not in their route"); single scull races; a grand-stand accident at the Cincinnati Union base-ball grounds; Victor Martin's proposed Paris-to-Rome walk; and the Union League's contract suits, including Tony Mullane.
articles.summary: A column of clipped national sporting news, with one local quip about the Bad Lands.

articles.headline: DICKINSON NOTES.
articles.text:
DICKINSON, Dak., May 13, 1884.

About 25,000 pounds of freight were forwarded from here over the new freight route Tuesday.

The party engaged in laying out the road have passed the north Cannon Ball and report a good road to and beyond that point.

The delegation selected to confer with the Black Hills merchants, returned Monday and report progress. Prospects for freight are looking favorably at this point.

The R. R. Co. is replacing the dam on the Heart river, which was damaged by the ice last winter. The substantial structure in process of erection, together with the new pump started last week, will insure a permanent water supply at this point.

The funeral of Mrs. Robt. Fuller took place on Saturday, after which Mr. Fuller left with the body for his former home in New York. Mr. and Mrs. Hayes received the sad intelligence Saturday that their son, a promising boy of seven years, had died suddenly of brain fever. Both Mr. Fuller and Mr. and Mrs. Hayes have the sympathy of the entire community in their afflictions.

Lieut. Varnum, of the 7th U. S. cavalry, in command of the force detailed to survey the freight route from Ft. Mead to Dickinson, arrived Monday morning. The party was delayed at the Belle Fourche by storms for some days. The Lieut. reports a very direct and practicable route and will officially report one of less than 190 miles. The party will remain here till late in the week, awaiting supplies from Ft. Lincoln, after which they will proceed to Medora in order to view a road from that point.

ANTHROPOS.
articles.summary: Dickinson correspondent 'Anthropos' (May 13) reports freight shipped over the new Black Hills route, road survey progress, the Heart river dam, two deaths, and Lieut. Varnum's survey party from Ft. Meade.

articles.headline: STOCK NOTES.
articles.text:
Press dispatches from various points in Texas show a large increase in the number of fine bulls being placed on the ranges.—[Breeder's Gazette.

Indications point to the removal of a good many herds of cattle from Indian territory to northern ranges the coming season. Grass in that country is still abundant, but legislation is averse to the stock interests.—[Breeder's Gazette.

Mr. Burke, of Burke & Jackson of Dallas, started a herd of 3,000 two-year-old steers from Hillsboro, Texas, on the 15th for the Yellowstone region in Montana. They go by way of Greer county and the Panhandle.—[Texas Live Stock Journal.

J. W. Snyder left last week for Texas and will start six to ten thousand head of two and three-year-old steers from the company's Stonewall ranch for the L F range in South park. They hope to leave the 15th to the 20th of June.—[Cheyenne Live Stock Journal.

A St. Louis dispatch says that advices from western Texas are to the effect that cattle are suffering, and large numbers are dying for want of water and grass, the drouth having been very severe in that section. Myriads of caterpillars have appeared and are destroying all kinds of vegetation.—[Black Hills Times.

The papers of New Mexico are happy over the great influx of Texas cattlemen. They are going in by the dozen and in a very short time that country will be filled with live, progressive men, who will join hands with the older ranchmen and make the grazing fields of that territory productive to their fullest capacity.—[N. W. L. S. Journal.

In district No. 10, which is the largest round-up cattle district in the State, there are estimated to be about 3,500 bulls. When they are all gathered together in one pasture, as they will be the coming fall, there will be music in the air. Nine of every ten of these bulls are graded Short-horns, with a sprinkling of Herefords, Holsteins and Polled-Angus.—[Colorado Live Stock Record.

Jos. Cuenin, Gunnison. Colo., writes: "I note an article in the last number of your paper that the Montana stockmen propose to adopt the plan of taking bulls off the range at certain seasons of the year. This agrees with the view I have entertained for some time past and I think the proposition, if carried into effect, will prove to be of value in the interest of stock growing.—[Breeder's Gazette.

An exchange says that young horses should never have shoes imposed upon them until it is well proved that they cannot do without them. He predicts that the day is not far off when some humane benefactor of his kind and horse-kind will procure a breed of horses having such firm, tough feet, in addition to all other good qualities, that shoeing will be unnecessary.—[N. W. Live Stock Journal.

The fact that should be borne in mind by those engaged in horse training is that the horse has a very acute faculty for understanding and interpreting the tone of the voice. If you talk confidently the animal acquires confidence, if your voice shows fear he notices it and is afraid. Talk kindly to your horse and be sure that he understands the meaning of the tone if not of the words.—[Exchange.

The loss among cattle during the past year is the greatest for several years. Mr. Longendyke and also Mr. J. H. Baker estimate their loss at about ten per cent. Their winter losses will probably reach as high as six or eight per cent. These are fair representaitons of losses among ranch herded cattle generally in this locality. They have resulted principally from the fact of the late fall rains destroying the nutritive qualities of the grass and are confined, to a very large extent, to cattle that were brought in here in the late summer or fall from eastern Kansas, Missouri and Iowa. Notwithstanding these great losses, stockmen are by no means discouraged. They say that the profits arising from increase in young stock and increased growth of the same will yet give them a good round profit for their year's work and investment. Some say that the loss may amount to as much as fifteen, twenty or even twenty-five per cent. and still a profit can be realized.—[Kansas Cowboy.

Never in the history of Montana did the horse interest look so encouraging as now. A larger number of well-bred stallions and mares will be brought into the territory this year than any previous season and never did our people manifest such an interest in the equine race as now. So great is the progress that we feel assured that the time is not far distant when our oft-repeated assertion that Montana roadsters and flyers will eclipse the world, is near at hand. This is no idle boast; on the contrary, it is based upon a train of facts that can scarcely fail to lead to such results. In the first place, we have a hilly country and the soil of our pastural lands is rocky and sandy and grows the clear, tough-hoof, ivory-like bone, powerful muscle ligaments and tendons that are an [illegible] on with the horses grown upon that soft, rich soil of the states. This, coupled with the rarity of our atmosphere, so improves the endurance and action as to warrant our conclusions. Even the horse bred in the states improves greatly by a few years' residence here, and after we have grown a few generations of high blood, if we have not a race of horses that will be sought for and [nerve?] for service, long endurance and superior achievements, and if they do not step away from anything grown elsewhere, we miss our guess and the low lands can walk away with our money.—[Husbandman.
articles.summary: Clipped range and livestock paragraphs from western stock papers: Texas bulls and drouth, herds moving north, round-up district bulls, horse care, cattle losses, and Montana horse breeding.

articles.text: Smoke the Far West.
articles.summary: Advertising line for the Far West cigar.

articles.text: Peter Malloy returned last Friday night from his eastern trip.
articles.summary: Peter Malloy returned Friday night from his eastern trip.

articles.text: Geo. Fitzgerald has been making some improvements in the Hotel de Mores.
articles.summary: Geo. Fitzgerald has been improving the Hotel de Mores.

articles.text: Geo. Smith was bitten severely last Saturday by the Kentucky stallion.
articles.summary: Geo. Smith was badly bitten by the Kentucky stallion.

articles.text: Al. Gifford stopped over a train Tuesday on his way to New York. He will return in two weeks.
articles.summary: Al. Gifford stopped over on his way to New York.

articles.text: Geo. Porter started for Chicago last Saturday to buy a $10,000 general stock of goods for the company.
articles.summary: Geo. Porter went to Chicago to buy a $10,000 stock of goods for the company.

articles.text: Lee Eisenberg, of Bismarck, travelling for Dan Eisenberg, was in town Monday and secured a number of orders.
articles.summary: Lee Eisenberg of Bismarck took orders in town Monday.

articles.text: There has been good fishing in the river for some time. Cat-fish and suckers are the principal ones caught.
articles.summary: Good fishing in the Little Missouri, mostly cat-fish and suckers.

articles.text: Smith & Graham's freight outfit arrived Monday from Montana. It consists of nine wagons and thirty-six mules.
articles.summary: Smith & Graham's nine-wagon, 36-mule freight outfit arrived from Montana.

articles.text: The COW BOY is feeling the effects of Medora's prosperity and job work is coming in as fast as we can take care of it.
articles.summary: The Cow Boy reports a rush of job printing.

articles.text: Ford's freighting outfit is on the way here from Helena. It is composed of twenty wagons and seventy-five mules.
articles.summary: Ford's 20-wagon, 75-mule freighting outfit is coming from Helena.

articles.text: There was great danger for awhile that the river would wash in too close to the slaughter-house but the building of the dam has averted it.
articles.summary: The new dam kept the river from washing too close to the slaughter-house.

articles.text: Wm. Byrd, the man who stole the team at Miles City, and who was arrested here last winter, was sentenced to five years in the penitentiary on the 7th.
articles.summary: Wm. Byrd, arrested at Medora for stealing a team at Miles City, got five years.

articles.text: Pat. O'Hara and wife are obeying the scriptural injunction to "multiply etc." to the best of their ability. The latest is a boy and arrived Tuesday morning.
articles.summary: Pat O'Hara and wife had a baby boy Tuesday.

articles.text: J. W. Reynolds, our printer, left Sunday morning for the east. Whoever employs him may be sure of getting as good a printer as there is in Dakota.
articles.summary: Printer J. W. Reynolds left for the east.

articles.text: Mr. A. Kyes was in town Saturday. He will soon be here all the time attending to the forwarding, which is now being done by Messrs. Bramble and VanTassel.
articles.summary: A. Kyes will take over freight forwarding now handled by Bramble and VanTassel.

articles.text: Part of the store room formerly used as a carriage house by the company has undergone a number of improvements and will be used temporarily as a meat market.
articles.summary: Part of the company's former carriage house will serve as a meat market.

articles.text: W. W. Duncan, of Mandan was in town on a business trip, the first of the week. He makes it pleasant for the boys and is in on the ground floor for all furniture orders from here.
articles.summary: W. W. Duncan of Mandan visited on furniture business.

articles.text: We wish we had as dead a cinch on a million dollars as Medora has on the freight route. It seems as though every freighting outfit in the country is heading this way.
articles.summary: The paper boasts that every freighting outfit is heading for Medora.

articles.text: J. Juelfs arrived Tuesday from Deadwood. He came on in advance of his outfit, which will probably be in to-day. It is made up of sixteen wagons and one hundred and six oxen.
articles.summary: J. Juelfs arrived from Deadwood ahead of his 16-wagon, 106-ox outfit.

articles.text: Ed. Kennedy, brother of Gill, arrived here from Adrian, Mich., last Saturday evening. He will take up his residence among us and engage in some kind of business. He is a welcome addition.
articles.summary: Ed. Kennedy, brother of Gill, arrived from Adrian, Mich., to settle.

articles.text: R. E. Spurrier has shipped his household goods to Spokane Falls and will start for that place as soon as a man arrives here to relieve him as agent. We are sorry to lose Mr. Spurrier, but rejoice at his promotion.
articles.summary: Agent R. E. Spurrier has been promoted and is moving to Spokane Falls.

articles.text: Bob. Roberts intends to bring back a number of passengers from Deadwood, paying them a large rebate if he does not make the return trip in six days. This will be fast time for heavy wagons but Bob. can make it if anyone can.
articles.summary: Bob Roberts offers passengers from Deadwood a rebate if his round trip takes over six days.

articles.text: Rassie Deffebach, of Spearfish, has rented the company's stable and will take possession June 1. Ras. is said to be as good a judge of cattle and horses as can be found in the west and he will be the right man in the right place.
articles.summary: Rassie Deffebach of Spearfish has rented the company's stable from June 1.

articles.text: An interesting wager was decided the first of the week between Wm. Vandriesche and Frank Keeler. William was to ride the bucker spoken of in another article, for half an hour. He won the bet but at the expense of a tumble or two.
articles.summary: Wm. Vandriesche won a bet with Frank Keeler by riding the bucker for half an hour.

articles.text: J. O'Sullivan, the barber, has bought a lot and next Monday will begin the erection of a barber shop. He will issue shaving tickets and we bespeak for him the hearty patronage that his skill as a barber and many good qualities as a gentleman demand.
articles.summary: Barber J. O'Sullivan bought a lot and will build a barber shop starting Monday.

articles.text: On account of the storm, but a small number turned out to hear Rev. Wm. Cooke's sermon at the Cantonment last Sunday evening. It is to be hoped that larger audiences will greet the reverend gentleman in the future. Both in public and private he is an interesting talker.
articles.summary: The storm kept attendance low at Rev. Wm. Cooke's Sunday sermon at the Cantonment.

articles.text: The dance at the Western house Monday evening for the benefit of C. E. Blake was largely attended. A snug sum was raised and will be sent to Mr. Blake, who is now in Miles City. Mr. Malloy furnished supper and his house free and Joe Delgie donated his services as musician.
articles.summary: A benefit dance for C. E. Blake was held at the Western House Monday evening.

articles.text: The largest and gumboist comment on the soon-to-be-abandoned freight route from Dickinson to the Hills is furnished by an eight-mule team, which was twenty-five days going from Dickinson to Mattock's, about fifty miles. During the same time Bob. Roberts took an outfit of twenty-seven wagons from Medora to Mattock's in less than two days. This settles the gumbo question. The team from Dickinson started some time before the snow and rain storm of ten days ago and Roberts started a couple of days after it. The time of the Dickinson outfit is vouched for by J. C. Ryan, of Spearfish, and that of Roberts by any one at Mattock's and by several persons here.
articles.summary: An eight-mule team took 25 days from Dickinson to Mattock's while Bob Roberts took 27 wagons from Medora in under two days.

articles.text: Our local page "can't stand the pressure" this week and "slops over" on the editorial page. On this account, the usual amount of editorial had to be omitted.
articles.summary: The local page overflowed onto the editorial page this week.

articles.text: We feel rather proud of this issue of the COW BOY as every stroke of work both literary and mechanical was done by "ye editor" since Monday morning. During the three days we have also turned out over $25 worth of job work. We are thinking of running a supplement next issue, just for recreation.
articles.summary: Packard did all the literary and mechanical work on this issue himself since Monday.

articles.text: Several of the horses brought down by Johnny Goodall have been broken at the Sully Creek ranch. As there are two or three steep embankments near the ranch and the horses take it into their heads to seek tall timber in almost any direction, it was deemed best to do the rest of the breaking at Beaver creek.
articles.summary: Horses brought down by Johnny Goodall are being broken, now at Beaver creek.

articles.text: T. G. Jones, of Deadwood, arrived last Monday evening. He took it easy on a valuable horse and made the distance in less than three days. Tuesday evening he went to Miles City but expects to return to-morrow. While here he purchased four of our best business lots, showing conclusively the faith he has in Medora.
articles.summary: T. G. Jones of Deadwood rode in Monday, bought four business lots, and went to Miles City.

articles.text: J. A. Beaumont, better known as "Scotty," is certainly having a streak of hard luck. Late last week his shack at the sheep ranch burned, together with all he owned. Coming to town to get a new outfit he received a letter from Scotland stating that his father was dead. "It never rains but it pours," is little consolation but "Scotty" may be sure that in his present affliction he has the heartfelt sympathy of all his friends.
articles.summary: J. A. 'Scotty' Beaumont's shack at the sheep ranch burned and he learned of his father's death.

articles.text: Particular attention is called to the advertisement of Peter J. Book, appearing for the first time in this issue. Mr. Book wishes it distinctly understood that he is making as good brick as can be made in America and will compete with any one in quality and price. There is a cement in the clay that dries and burns perfectly without a crack or blemish and without the use of sand in any of the processes of making. Both white and red, mould and re-pressed brick will be made, and extensive pottery works will be built in the fall, thus furnishing employment to a large force of men the year round. Besides being a brick-maker Mr. Book is an experienced contractor and is just the kind of energetic business man that makes a valuable citizen.
articles.summary: Peter J. Book's Medora brick and planned pottery works are promoted.

articles.text: The cattlemen are all supposed to know that the round-up for this section of the Bad Lands begins May 25, at the Beaver creek crossing of the N. P. R. R. Every stock owner will send enough cowboys to look after his interests, who will all be under the orders of and subject to dismissal by the foreman, John Goodall. Each cattle owner will provide a mess-wagon or make arrangements to mess with some one else. At least six good horses will be needed by every man. There will be day and night herding, in which each man must take part. Branding will be done every day. Every man who wishes his cattle taken care of, must be represented on the round-up. The time taken by the round-up will be from six weeks to two months and the extent of territory is about one hundred by fifty miles. In this district there are about 40,000 cattle.
articles.summary: The Bad Lands round-up begins May 25 at the Beaver creek crossing under foreman John Goodall.

articles.text: The cattle belonging to H. B. Wadsworth & Co. came in last Friday. They consisted of 1,333 yearling and two-year-old heifers, all in good condition. They are all Minnesota cattle and from the time they were bought, shipped here, driven to the ranch and up to the present not a head was lost from any cause. Together with the cattle, came several brood mares and a valuable stallion. Before this shipment there were 1,500 cattle on the range and Mr. M. Wadsworth has not seen a dead animal there and knows where all but ten or a dozen of them are. Every cattle paper that we see, estimates the loss at from three to thirty per cent. and we challenge the United States to equal Mr. Wadsworth's record. At the outside it does not equal one-tenth of one per cent. There is not a newspaper in the country but that would rejoice at the smallness of a loss thirty times as great. Bring the banner to the Bad Lands.
articles.summary: H. B. Wadsworth & Co. received 1,333 Minnesota heifers without a loss.

articles.text: Perfecto Fernandez, the Mexican who returned with Johnny Goodall, is a rider from way back. One of the horses is like Mark Train's racer: "warranted to out-buck anything in America." After throwing several riders, the Mexican mounted him. An amused smile began to spread over the bronco's face but it didn't percolate far. His first move was to jump straight into the air and come down stiff-legged, as solid as a brick house. The Mexican never budged but got out his paper and tobacco and began rolling a cigarette. This, the reader will understand, is not always necessary nor, we might add, customary. We have actually seen men on bucking horses who seemed to have their hands full enough without rolling a cigarette. As a general rule we have noticed that the rider seemed, so to speak, to be confining his attention strictly to sticking on. About the time the cigarette got to going, the bronco began to think that his reputatien was at stake. As a preliminary, he jumped into the air, threw down his head and landed on his front legs with a shock sufficient to unseat the throne of grace. Perfecto took a puff at his cigarette, put his foot up by the bronco's ear and rolled him clear to his flank with his stirrup. This was done to encourage the bucker which seemed to think that in some way he had missed the combination. It did put more life into the entertainment for the bronco started on a new deal and began turning forward and back double somersaults with a facility that would put a trained athlete to the blush. Perfecto merely threw his leg over the pommel and rode side-saddle fashion. He really shouldn't have done this for it broke the broncho up in business. He would and could out-buck anything in America but he couldn't buck against fate. He immediately and unanimously soured on himself and since then has never bucked a solitary buck.
articles.summary: Perfecto Fernandez rode a notorious bucking bronco while rolling a cigarette.

articles.text: The first car-load of Columbia river salmon passed through here Monday morning on No. 2. It was gaudily labeled and will be run through to New York on fast time. The Marquis has a contract to furnish two car-loads a week to a New York house, of which the above is the first shipment.
articles.summary: The first car-load of Columbia river salmon under the Marquis's New York contract passed through eastbound.
